video_title: Why “everyone’s a builder” isn’t working | A reality check with Sherif Mansour
gist: Atlassian's head of AI and product craft Sherif Mansour argues the 'everyone's an AI builder' narrative failed in practice: an internal Atlassian experiment of builder-only squads reverted to traditional roles within a month because AI makes throughput cheap and direction the bottleneck, which helps explain Lenny's data showing PM openings leading tech hiring. He also argues for hiring artist PMs and AI-native juniors, bolting agents onto existing Jira workflows (nearly 10M agent runs per month), and treating design and experience as the main differentiator.

themes.theme: AI builders vs. direction: why PM demand is rising

insights.claim: Lenny's forthcoming state-of-the-tech-job-market report finds PM has the most open roles of any tech function in the AI era, while engineering openings are slowing, design is flat and user research is weak (only ~108 open UXR roles globally at tech companies).
insights.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
insights.so_what: Contradicts the 'PMs are obsolete' narrative; labor-market tools and PM-focused SaaS may see steadier demand than engineering-seat-based tools.
insights.quote: There's uh a hundred open roles for user research globally at tech companies right now. A hundred eight a hundred and eight.

insights.claim: Atlassian ran experimental squads of PMs and designers acting purely as 'AI builders' with no PM or designer role; velocity felt unprecedented for a few weeks, but within about a month everyone reverted to their traditional jobs.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Evidence that 'everyone becomes a builder' collapses in practice at scale; be skeptical of headcount-collapse theses built on it.
insights.quote: after about a month he comes back and he's like everyone's gone back to doing their traditional jobs.

insights.claim: At companies with dozens to thousands of engineers, AI makes throughput cheap so the bottleneck shifts to direction/alignment, increasing demand for people who 'steer the ship' (PMs) rather than more code output.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: As AI commoditizes code throughput, value accrues to coordination/alignment layers and tools, not raw code generation volume.
insights.quote: we realize throughput's not our problem. Directions are problem. But throughput's getting cheaper.

insights.claim: Sherif's internal Atlassian guidance to PMs is 'direct the ship, don't row it': shipping production code is rarely the PM's bottleneck, except in startups and zero-to-one projects where AI-builder generalists make sense.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Distinguish startup/0-to-1 contexts (generalist builders win) from scaled orgs (direction is scarce) when evaluating AI-builder tooling adoption claims.
insights.quote: I wrote this blog post internally that was, you know, direct the ship, don't row it.

insights.claim: AI amplifies existing strengths and weaknesses rather than merging roles: like the Balsamiq mockup era, everyone can prototype, but PMs remain poor solution designers, so specialist skill circles all grow without overlapping.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Role-convergence theses (one 'builder' replacing PM/design/eng) are overstated; specialist tools and talent retain value.
insights.quote: PMs are some of the worst solution designers in the world.

insights.claim: You can only get AI to produce output as good as your own knowledge of the specialization, because effective prompting requires domain expertise.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Supports durable demand for domain experts as AI quality gatekeepers.
insights.quote: you can only get the AI to do something as good as your knowledge of the specialization is

insights.claim: PMs should first diagnose the team's context gap (customer, vision, market) and only then pick AI tools to close it, e.g. prototyping for vision gaps or dispatching agents for market analysis.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: AI PM-tool adoption is problem-led; vendors that map to specific context gaps should outperform generic 'make PMs code' tools.

themes.theme: PM role: context-filling and decision velocity

insights.claim: In medium-to-large orgs the PM's main job is filling context gaps across three types (customer, product/market, and business) to build a 'shared brain' with the team, including AI agents.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Context is the scarce resource; knowledge-management and context-sharing platforms (e.g. Confluence) gain strategic value in the agent era.
insights.quote: you have the customer context, you have the product and market context, and you have the business that you operate in context.

insights.claim: PMs don't own decisions; they own decision-making velocity, pushing context to engineers and designers so they decide themselves, which is why Sherif tells PMs to 'stay away from the Jira backlog'.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Signals a shift from ticket-centric work management to context-centric collaboration; watch how Atlassian positions Jira versus Confluence/Rovo.
insights.quote: PMs own decision making velocity.

insights.claim: Scaling product teams beyond roughly 20-30 people is the hardest thing Sherif has done in 17 years at Atlassian, because trust and shared context break and us-vs-them culture forms.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Org scale is a key execution risk for fast-growing software companies; context-sharing practices are a leading indicator.
insights.quote: In any scaled organization more than 20 30 people you're going to run into this.

insights.claim: Bringing engineers into customer interviews produced Confluence's in-page task checkbox in 2010: an engineer saw customers using red/green star icons as manual task markers and proposed native checkboxes.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Example of paving manual customer workarounds into product features, a repeatable source of product edge.

insights.claim: The PM craft triangle (created by Geoff Redfern) classifies PMs as general manager (TAM/revenue), scientist (hypothesis/A-B testing) or artist (vision/experience-led); Atlassian uses it in hiring and calibration, and few people excel at all three.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Useful lens for assessing product-org fit in management diligence: growth teams need scientists, 0-to-1 needs generalists.

insights.claim: Mismatched PMs often recover simply by switching to a project type that fits their archetype, so Sherif advises leaning into strengths and building complementary teams rather than fixing weaknesses.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Talent allocation, not headcount, drives product-team output.

insights.claim: Atlassian CEO/co-founder Mike is cited as a rare leader who critiques pixel-level design, business models and data in the same review.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Founder depth across design, business and data is a qualitative signal for Atlassian's product culture.

themes.theme: Hiring shift: artist PMs, taste, and AI-native juniors

insights.claim: Large orgs are increasingly hiring artist/experience-led PMs because taste matters more when everyone has access to the same intelligence.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: When AI commoditizes features, UX/taste becomes the differentiator; favor companies with strong design-led product orgs.
insights.quote: taste has become more important than ever before when everyone has access to the same intelligence.

insights.claim: As software becomes cheaper to build and vendors converge on similar features, experience becomes a primary differentiator; Sherif does not believe a chat-with-an-agent interface will be the single final interface.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Bearish on pure chat-UI commoditization theses; bullish on vendors with differentiated UX and multiple interfaces.
insights.quote: I'm not a believer that everyone's going to chat to an agent and the agent interface is the is the final interface.

insights.claim: Sherif pushes back on established organizations that think they no longer need to hire juniors; Atlassian has deliberately over-indexed on hiring juniors over seniors because AI-native juniors bring new ways of working to a workforce that must transform.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Contrary to 'AI kills entry-level jobs' narrative; watch junior hiring at incumbents as a sign of AI transformation strategy.
insights.quote: we have definitely overindexed on hiring more juniors than seniors

insights.claim: Atlassian research found juniors are roughly 38% more likely than seniors to adopt new AI tools, while seniors extract better quality and productivity from the tools they do use but are less willing to change workflows.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: AI tool adoption curves differ by seniority; seat expansion may come from juniors, monetized value from seniors.
insights.quote: I think it's 38% posted a blog about it but like of juniors are more likely to adopt new tools than the seniors

insights.claim: Juniors can't easily spot AI slop because they lack domain expertise, while seniors catch it quickly, so the optimal AI-era workforce pairs juniors (experimentation/demos) with seniors (evals, quality).
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Eval and quality-control tooling demand rises as AI-native juniors ship more output.

insights.claim: Atlassian runs 'AI builder weeks' where all crafts stop normal work to tinker with AI tools for a week.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Signals heavy internal AI-adoption investment at a major enterprise software vendor.

insights.claim: Lenny's data shows designer hiring stagnant; Sherif's hypothesis is the market hasn't yet realized experience matters most in AI, and at Atlassian design has never played a bigger role in roadmap driving in his 17 years there.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Possible mispricing of design talent; Lenny frames it as 'buy low' on designers.
insights.quote: design has never played a more important role in roadmap driving than ever before.

themes.theme: Atlassian AI strategy: Rovo and agents in workflows

insights.claim: Atlassian sees nearly 10 million agents running in loops every month inside Jira and Confluence, handling tasks like triage, code generation and legal contract review.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Concrete agent-usage scale metric for Atlassian (TEAM); track as an AI monetization KPI.
insights.quote: we have like nearly 10 million agents that run in loops every every month inside Jira and Confluence

insights.claim: Atlassian launched general Rovo Chat and user-built Rovo Agents about three and a half years ago instead of only point features, using the open 'canvas' to discover use cases and then productize common ones (e.g. grouping whiteboard sticky notes, native AI triage).
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: 'Paving the cow path' lets incumbents with usage data identify which agent use cases to productize natively, an advantage over startups.

insights.claim: Customers have modeled billions of business workflows in Jira, much of it by non-software teams (e.g. app-store approvals, telecom complaint handling), giving Atlassian a large surface to insert agents.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Jira's installed workflow base is a distribution moat for agentic AI; supports bull case on Atlassian AI attach.
insights.quote: customers have billions of workflows already modeled on on our platform

insights.claim: For established products, 'bolting on' AI to existing workflows is the best way to become AI-native, rather than rewriting from scratch; Atlassian lets users add agents to Jira workflow columns and cards.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Incumbents with entrenched workflows can migrate users from AI novice to AI native incrementally, countering 'AI-native startups disrupt incumbents' thesis.
insights.quote: the best way to reinvent your product to be AI native is to understand the flows that exist in your product and literally bolt on AI to them.

insights.claim: Gemini integrated into Google Maps (incl. Apple CarPlay in Australia) illustrates 'workflow proximity': users engage AI in-context rather than switching apps.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Distribution via existing high-usage surfaces favors incumbents like Google embedding AI into owned workflows.
insights.quote: it's such a lesson in product workflow proximity.

insights.claim: Starting from existing assets is a valid product-strategy method: list current assets and beliefs and connect them, as Amazon extended a huge-inventory bookstore into the everything store.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Look for companies leveraging unique existing assets into adjacent markets.

insights.claim: Sherif warns that with AI, teams are not talking to humans enough because it has become easier to stay behind dashboards.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Qualitative customer insight may become scarcer and more valuable.

themes.theme: Open-by-default culture and remote work as AI context

insights.claim: Atlassian is open by default (most exec reviews recorded and searchable), which Sherif argues compounds in the AI era because more documented context is available to both AI and humans.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Companies with rich written/documented context may realize more AI productivity; favorable for knowledge-base vendors.
insights.quote: having an open by default approach to things is actually better in the long run for you as a company

insights.claim: Atlassian data scientists are testing the hypothesis that remote employees get more outcomes from AI than co-located ones, because remote workers write and share more digitally.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: If proven, it is a counterpoint to return-to-office mandates and a tailwind for async collaboration tools.
insights.quote: those that are remote are more likely to get uh more outcomes out of AI then those are co-located.

insights.claim: Lenny's report shows remote work has plateaued at roughly 10-20% across industries.
insights.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
insights.so_what: Watch whether AI reaccelerates remote share; relevant to collaboration-software TAM.
insights.quote: remote work has plateaued. There's no it's kind of stalled at 10 15 20% across industries

themes.theme: Leadership, career ladders and working with founders

insights.claim: Atlassian runs dual-track career paths with distinguished PMs and engineers contributing at exec level, and people switch between IC and manager tracks; manager span of control is at least 3-4, with most around 8-9.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Organizational design detail for Atlassian; IC paths help retain senior talent.

insights.claim: The most common failure of new PM managers is going hands-off too quickly; the best managers lead by example in product reviews, which Sherif expects to matter more with AI.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Hands-on leadership is a quality signal when assessing product orgs.

insights.claim: In Sherif's experience, visionary founders/stakeholders have been right about 99% of the time because they have thought longest about the domain, so the job is to catch up to their reasoning ('chapter 10') and then bring the team along.
insights.speaker: Sherif Mansour
insights.so_what: Supports backing founder-led enterprise software companies with long domain tenure.
insights.quote: My my experience they've been right 99% of the time.

insights.claim: Lenny cites Dharmesh Shah's 'flash tags' (FYI, suggestion, recommendation, plea) for signaling conviction; Sherif says PMs should ask stakeholders to clarify their conviction level when they don't tag it.
insights.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
insights.so_what: Communication framework for decision clarity in founder-led companies.
